title: SDK stream partitioning and tool contracts — PRD sketch
content:
Context and objective:
This is a working PRD sketch for a combined Hosted API feature: partitioned streaming (fast/mid/full tiers), a declarative tool binding contract for low-latency tool calls during incremental output, and SDK ergonomic patterns for clients to integrate progressive structured output without hard failure modes. Goal: reduce mean time-to-first-useable-token (TTFUT) for embedded clients while keeping token cost predictable and making tool integrations safe and easy for external developers.

Background / motivation:
- Many customers want deterministic, fast partial outputs for interactive UIs (search assistants, code-editors, chat widgets) while still being able to call tools mid-stream (QA, DB lookups, code execution).
- Current streaming surfaces either stream everything slowly (good fidelity, bad latency) or aggressively buffer (bad UX for micro-interactions).
- Tool calling today is request-level: clients call tools after a final response, or we offer streaming tool events that are heavyweight to integrate.
- SDK ergonomics requests: simple client APIs that: subscribe to incremental frames, declaratively register tool capabilities and their estimated latency/cost, and receive structured partial outputs with graceful degradation.

Principles we should follow:
- Predictable latency tiers: expose fast/mid/full streaming lanes with clear cost/quality tradeoffs.
- Declarative capability negotiation: tool contracts should be advertised and negotiated at session start so the runtime can plan prefetching and hedging.
- Non-blocking stream progress: tool call slowdowns should not stall progressive delivery of best-effort text/structured frames.
- Observability-first: surface per-frame telemetry (lateness, tool resolution events, cache hits) to Console and per-token cost attribution.

Proposal summary (high level):
1) Stream partitioning: server partitions incremental output into three lanes:
   - fast: minimal tokens, aggressive truncation/abstraction, prioritized for latency-sensitive UI updates.
   - mid: more context, short expansions, suitable for follow-on user interactions.
   - full: final detailed output and structured payloads (JSON blocks, action sequences).
   The client opts into lanes per-route or per-session. By default we deliver fast frames as soon as partial logits cross low-confidence thresholds.

2) Declarative tool contracts (session-level):
   - SDK exposes a simple register_tools(session_config) call where each tool declares: id, input_schema, max_expected_latency_ms (p50/p95), cost_estimate, idempotency_token_hint.
   - Server schedules speculative prefetch or KV-cache lookups for tools with low latency and marks tools with high latency as asynchronous: tool results come back as separate event frames that the client can stitch in or present as an attachment.
   - Tool call policy options: inline-sync (block full lane), async-attachment (emit placeholder in fast/mid, attach result later), speculative-merge (runtime fuses tool result into mid lane if latency < threshold).

3) Structured partial outputs:
   - Frame format: incremental frames carry: lane, cursor_id, sequence, optional structured_payload (small JSONL snippet or schema-typed block), provenance meta (which model variant produced it), and tool-resolution hint.
   - Content negotiation for structure: client can request one of: plain-text-first, json-first, mixed-with-summaries. The server will attempt to produce the requested shape progressively.

4) SDK ergonomics (developer-facing):
   - Client API sketch (pseudo):
       session = Redwood.hosted.create_session(route='chat', lanes=['fast','mid','full'], tool_contracts=[...])
       session.on('frame', handler) // receives frames with lane and structure
       session.register_tools([...]) // optional mid-session tool additions
       session.commit_action(action_id) // for structured action frames
   - High-level SDK helpers: FrameAdapter (maps frames to UI diff/patch), ToolProxy (wraps tool call and implements idempotency/hedging automatically), FallbackPolicies (client chooses fast-only fallback).
   - Mobile-first considerations: allow disabling mid/full lanes for low-bandwidth and expose compact frames with deltas only.

5) Observability and telemetry:
   - Emit per-frame logs: frame_id, lane, emitted_at, model_variant, tokens_emitted, tool_events[] (tool_id, start, end, cache_hit boolean).
   - Console: new per-route streaming dashboard showing lane distribution, average time-to-first-fast-frame, mid/final merge rate, and tool latency heatmaps.
   - Billing: attribute tokens and tool-execution cost to the lane that produced them; show a lane-level cost breakdown.

API examples (very rough):
- Create session (HTTP POST):
  { route: "chat", lanes: ["fast","mid","full"], tools: [{id:"search",schema:{q:string},p50:80,p95:450}] }
- Sample frame (server -> client over socket):
  { frame_id: "f-123", lane: "fast", seq: 2, text: "We found two results:", structured: null }
- Tool result event (later):
  { event: "tool_result", tool_id: "search", tool_request_id: "tr-11", result: {items:[...]}, attach_to_frame: "f-123" }

Rollout plan / milestones:
- Phase 0 (experiment): internal SDK clients only. Implement fast/mid lane, frame format v0 (no tool contracts). 6 weeks.
- Phase 1 (contracted tools): add declarative tool contract shape, implement speculative-merge and async-attachment modes. 8–10 weeks.
- Phase 2 (public beta): SDK shipped with FrameAdapter + ToolProxy helpers, telemetry plumbing to Console. 6 weeks.
- Phase 3 (GA): increase backward compatibility and on-by-default for hosted routes; billing lanes stable. 4 weeks.

Key metrics / success criteria:
- Time-to-first-fast-frame median reduced by >= 40% for target routes.
- % of sessions that receive a fast-frame within 200ms of request > 70% (for low-latency routes).
- Tool-inlined merge rate (speculative merge success) > 50% for tools with p95 < 300ms.
- Developer adoption: 10 pilot customers onboarded in beta with SDK integration examples.

Acceptance criteria (for beta):
- Stable frame format v1 documented (examples + schemas).
- SDK helpers in official JS + Python SDKs with unit tests and examples.
- Console has lane-level telemetry and cost breakdown for pilot customers.
- No regressions in hosted API SLOs (95th latency for non-streamed endpoints).

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: complexity of merging speculative tool outputs could produce inconsistent final outputs.
  Mitigation: require tools to provide idempotency hints and provenance; default to async-attachment unless spec-merge confidence threshold reached.
- Risk: Clients misuse lanes (over-request fast lane causing cost spikes).
  Mitigation: soft quotas and heuristics in runtime; telemetry alerts and per-route default lane caps.
- Risk: Increased operational load for Console telemetry ingestion.
  Mitigation: sample frames by route severity and provide a low-volume default telemetry policy.

Open questions / decisions to make:
- Do we expose lane QoS as hard SLOs per tenant or as best-effort with SLA only for Dedicated tiers? (Prefer Dedicated SLOs.)
- How strict should tool schema validation be at registration vs runtime? (Prefer lightweight validation at registration with optional runtime validation hooks.)
- What is the default lane set for 'chat' vs 'complete' routes? (Propose fast+mid for chat, full only optional.)

Implementation notes / engineering considerations:
- Runtime should maintain per-session plan: mapping of tool_id -> preferred strategy (inline/speculative/async). Allows autoscaler to pre-assign GPU worklets or prewarm caches.
- Storage: small ephemeral attachments stored in S3-like store with attachment ids returned in stream events. Attachments should be GC'ed after X days.
- Backwards compatibility: older SDKs receive only 'full' lane frames when not negotiated.

Next steps (short term):
- Product: finalize lane names and default per-route configs.
- SDK: prototype FrameAdapter in JS playground + add simple mock tool-proxy.
- Eng: spike runtime plan structure and speculative-merge heuristics (2 x 2-week spikes).
- UX: create a quick demo (chat widget) showing fast-first + attached tool results.

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Mockup wireframe for consumer chat UI using lane patches.
- Create perf test harness to measure TTFUT with synthetic workload.
- Coordinate with billing to model lane-cost math.

End of sketch. This doc intentionally leaves many details open — focusing on an opinionated but pragmatic end-to-end surface that reduces latency while making tool calls safe and observable.
